segments: The 11th Dynasty
of the Arab Kings, and burned the gate of 'Amkawa.
And the Babylonians (Baghdadis) entered Erbil,
and pillaged (or: they pillaged?) it.
And after a little while, the Babylonians gained control also over its citadel.
And Shams al-Din Batkin became governor over it,
and as 'arid al-jaysh (inspector of the army),
a noble man whose name was Abu'l-Ma'ali Muhammad bar Nasir Salaya, and Mushrif bar Sadaqah
and Lu'lu', lord of Mosul.
And in the year 1544
of the Greeks, an imperial patent (sigillion) of kingship was written for Badr al-Din, lord of Mosul, by the Caliph,
and he was proclaimed Sultan,
because that young boy,
Nasir al-Din Mahmud, son of (read:) Qahir, son of Nur al-Din,
had already died.
The sons of al-'Adil, however, were very indignant with Sultan 'Ala al-Din because he had taken Khilat from them,
and gathered (or: they gathered?) a large assembly from Egypt as far as Aleppo (Beroea).
And there allied with the Egyptians also the lord of Hisn Ziyad (Kharput),
and the lord of Mardin,
and the lord of Mosul,
and al-Malik al-Afdal, son of Saladin, the lord of Samosata,
a multitude of the Ma'addites (nomadic Arabs),
and also the Taghlibites.
The Sultan also, in turn, gathered a great force of Franks, Greeks, Armenians, Georgians (Iberians), and Khwarazmians,
more than one hundred thousand, all of them picked warriors,
in the year one thousand
five hundred and forty-five of the Greeks (1545).
And he led them and went to the region of Albastan,
where the Egyptians and those with them were about to enter.
And when the sons of al-'Adil sent spies,
and saw that they were no match for the Sultan's army,
they went and took Hisn Mansur,
and devastated its entire territory,
and then their assembly was dispersed,
and they returned to their own territory.
And that Sultan came to Melitene with the great army that was with him,
and from there he crossed the Euphrates,
and went and encamped against Hisn Ziyad,
and quickly gained control over the city and plundered it.
Its lord, however, along with six thousand horsemen from the Egyptians who had come to his aid,
fled and went into the citadel of the city.
And the Sultan set up mangonels against them.
And when they were hard pressed by fighting, hunger, and thirst,
they received a promise (of quarter) for their lives.
Now the Sultan, to those Egyptians,
whose leader was Shams {OCR?}
